And when I actually sit down and compare the timestamps on the hospital's internal logs with the server routing data on those donation emails... they don't match. Not even close. There are gaps. So, no. I'm not mistaken. When you take the timestamps, the missing attachments, and the highly evasive behavior of the people involved... it’s obvious to me. turns.doctor_question: Aside from your father’s death, have you had any other fixed beliefs that people were hiding or tampering with information?
turns.patient_response:
Other beliefs? No, no. See, that's exactly my point, Doctor. I don't just go around inventing conspiracies or looking for shadows in every corner of my life. I'm not a paranoid person. My work, my finances, my day-to-day interactions—everything else is completely normal and above board. I don't think the barista is tampering with my coffee or the IRS is hiding my tax returns. It is *only* this specific, highly documented situation regarding my father. 

And I wouldn't even call it a "fixed belief." It's a conclusion based on empirical evidence. I know everyone keeps telling me that the hospital records and the donation emails all line up perfectly. My family, the hospital administrators, the charity board—they all look at these surface-level, flattened PDFs and tell me it's a closed case, that everything is standard procedure. But they aren't looking at the raw data the way I am. 

When I actually sit down and compare the timestamps on those server logs... I mean, you can literally see where the sequence breaks. And then there are the missing attachments that were clearly scrubbed from the email chain before it was forwarded to me. You don't just lose a 4-megabyte attachment in transit without a bounce-back error. It was manually removed. 

And then, of course, you add in the human element, right? The behavioral anomalies. The way certain community members—people who were heavily involved with his estate and the fundraising—the way they completely avoid my questions. I send a simple, polite email asking for a basic technical clarification on a routing number, and suddenly they take three weeks to reply, or they CC a legal representative, or they just physically turn and walk the other way when they see me. You don't do that if the records actually line up. You just answer the question. 

So, no, I don't have a history of thinking people are tampering with things. But in this one, specific instance? It’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. The data proves it, the behavioral patterns prove it, and I'm just the only one actually willing to parse the logs and look at it.

I don't lose touch with my surroundings or suddenly feel like it's happening all over again. Like I was saying before, there was no trauma in the actual moment of his passing. It was a very quiet, very expected cessation of biological function. I was sitting right there in the vinyl chair, holding his hand. It wasn't violent or sudden, so there's no psychological trigger for a flashback, you know? It’s just a standard, sequential memory stored in my brain.

What I *do* experience—and maybe this is what you're trying to get at, clinically speaking—is a very high degree of cognitive preoccupation. But it's not about his death itself. It's about the data surrounding the aftermath. 

I'll be sitting at my desk at work, supposedly compiling a completely unrelated systems health report for our regional manager, and my brain will just start looping through the hexadecimal values of that altered PDF header. I'll just be staring at my dual monitors, running the timeline over and over, trying to figure out how they managed to spoof the document creation date without triggering the hospital's automated audit trail. It’s incredibly distracting, yes, and it takes up a massive amount of my mental bandwidth during the day. Sometimes I have to literally get up and pace the server room just to burn off the sheer, frustrating energy it gives me, because I know the answer is right there in the logs if I can just find the right query to expose it. 

But that’s not a flashback. That’s just active, continuous problem-solving. That’s my brain refusing to let go of a glaring logical inconsistency. So, no, no flashbacks to the death itself. Just a lot of waking hours spent trying to untangle the digital mess they left behind.

It's incredibly frustrating because I'm just trying to show them the facts, and they treat me like I'm being difficult or obsessive. So, yes, the main place this whole situation causes friction is when I bring up my questions about my father’s records with family or community members. They just refuse to engage with the data, and that naturally creates a lot of tension. But as for my actual work or my daily activities? No, I'm functioning perfectly well. Better than most people, honestly, given the circumstances.
